The proposed fix is the smallest one that covers all three cases. Fixing only the account mismatch would miss the take-off case, where thread_id is already gone. Keeping thread_id on a taken-off row would hold on to identifiers taken from the mail's own headers, which is what take-off removes. So: work out the conversations before the change, from the chosen rows or from conversations_holding called at the key. Keep them for one message too, not only for a set (the_set_leaving only makes a set when more than one message leaves). Then hand them to the catch-up. Add a test for each case: a POP Inbox delete, a take-off, and a move to another account.

findings.title: In the message view, a message read from an opened conversation never turns read
findings.what_this_is: what_reading_may_mark (13.2-03.1) decides which message the reading timer may mark read. It accepts a member of the opened conversation only under conversation view.
findings.problem: In the message view, Enter on a threaded row opens the same conversation window. A member read there is never the cursor row's own message, and the conversation branch is skipped (`showing_conversations().then(...)??`), so it is never marked. The plan kept this 'as today', but nothing in the code or the changelog says so.
findings.concrete_case: Message view. Row A has a reply B. Enter on A, arrow to B, press Enter, read it past the wait, then close. B stays unread and the folder's unread count still counts it.
findings.fix: When the list shows messages, take the conversation (account and thread) from the cursor row's own loaded message instead of from s.conversations, and keep the rest of the check as it is.

REFUTED: The case is real but it is not a bug. It is the designed behaviour, and the proposed code fix would break a rule the project tests. (1) Nothing changed for the flat view in 13.2. Before 13.2-03.1, with the cursor on A and B opened from the conversation window, B was not marked read either. The doc comment on what_reading_may_mark at 0b781473 says the wider rule applies "Under conversation view" only. Plan 13.2-03.1 line 272 keeps the message view "as today". So this is a decision that is written down and tested, not an edge case someone missed. (2) The view gate exists for a reason. In the flat view A and B are separate rows. The selection handler is not allowed to touch reading_began (tests/moving_through_the_list_marks_nothing_read.rs), so the reading clock keeps running when the cursor moves. With the first proposed fix (treat the cursor row's thread as "the row's conversation"), pressing Space on unread B and then arrowing up to its parent A before the wait ends would mark B read after the cursor had left B's row. That breaks the #25 rule that the cursor must still be on the row the message was read from, and it turns the pinning test red. The state cannot tell "the cursor moved off B" from "B was opened from A's conversation window" without extra state, so the fix is not small and not safe. (3) The changelog says "as long as the list's cursor is still on that conversation's row". The flat view has no conversation rows, so the sentence is ambiguous but not plainly wrong. In the flat view B also has its own row, and reading B from that row marks it. At most this is a wording change to the changelog (add "under conversation view"), which is "nice", not a "should" bug. Load does not matter here.

findings.title: Marking many conversations scans every row against every touched one
findings.what_this_is: `bring_rows_up_to_date` (13.2-02) refreshes the conversation rows after a change made here, such as a mark, a star, a delete or an undo. It runs on the UI thread while holding the state lock.
findings.problem: For every row on screen it runs `touched.iter().find(..)`, a linear scan that compares two strings per entry. Rows the change did not touch, which is almost all of them, scan the whole touched list. The cost is rows on screen times conversations touched. 13.2-31.1 timed it with one conversation touched (22 to 35 ms over 22,503 rows) and never with a selection.
findings.concrete_case: A 200,000-message folder in conversation view has about 130,000 rows (the fixture ratio was 22,503 rows for 34,407 messages). Select 3,000 single-message rows (under the 5,000-message bound) and press M. That is about 130,000 x 3,000 = 3.9e8 `WhoseConversation::is` calls, each comparing the account id string and then the thread id. That is seconds with the state lock held on the UI thread. The window and the screen reader freeze, and so does every sync thread waiting on the lock.
findings.fix: Build lookups once: a `HashSet<(&str, &str)>` of touched (account_id, thread_id) pairs and a `HashMap<(&str, &str), &ConversationItem>` from `fresh`. Look each row up by its pair instead of scanning. About six lines, and the existing five tests still hold it.
findings.if_we_skip: A large selection marked, starred or deleted in conversation view freezes the app for seconds, and the cost grows with folder size times selection size.
findings.evidence: git show 0b781473:src/presentation/view_state.rs L290-313: `for (at, row) in on_screen.iter().enumerate() { let Some(this) = touched.iter().find(|one| one.is(row)) ... match fresh.iter().find(|came_back| this.is(came_back))`. git show 0b781473:src/application/conversations.rs L296-301: `is` compares account_id then thread_id strings. git show 0b781473:src/presentation/wx_app.rs L28106-28111: called with `&s.conversations` (every row) under `lock_state`. L12821-12822 and L12896-12897: mark and star pass every chosen message. git show 0b781473:src/application/editing.rs L122: MOST_ROWS_WORTH_SELECTING = 5_000. git show 0b781473:.planning/phases/13.2-the-audit-s-fixes/13.2-31.1-PLAN.md: 'the rule over 22,503 rows 35.0 ms', measured for one named conversation only.
checker_notes:
STANDS: The finding holds at 0b781473. I followed the path from M (toggle_read_state) with 3,000 conversation rows selected:
- chosen_messages builds the set.
- too_many(3,000) lets it through, because the limit is 5,000.
- mark_these_read runs, then bring_the_conversation_rows_up_to_date.
- conversations_holding returns all 3,000 conversations. It passes them as JSON, so no SQL variable limit cuts the list short.
- conversations_named_in returns 3,000 fresh rows.
- Then bring_rows_up_to_date(&s.conversations, &named, &fresh) runs on the UI thread with lock_state held.

Nothing on the way returns early, caps the size, or falls back to re-reading the whole folder.

For each of the ~130,000 rows, `touched.iter().find(|one| one.is(row))` checks every entry of the 3,000-long list for each row the change did not touch. In a single-folder view every row has the same account, so each `is` fully compares the 36-character account ID and then compares the thread ID. That is about 3.9e8 calls at a few nanoseconds each, so roughly 1 to 3 seconds with the lock held.

Two things make this function the main cost of such a press rather than a small addition:
- 13.2-31.1's SUMMARY puts the other per-conversation steps at about 0.07 ms each (about 0.25 s for 3,000).
- Its timing test passes `touched` from one 2-message conversation, so a selection was never measured.

Impact by size: at Pratik's 22,503-row inbox this is only about 0.4 to 0.7 s. It reaches seconds only near the 200,000-message load this review was asked to judge against.

A hash lookup keyed on (account_id, thread_id) makes the cost grow with rows plus touched instead of rows times touched. Group "should" (real slowness, not wrong output) is right.

Related but outside this finding: mark_these_read's per-message `s.messages.iter_mut().find` has the same rows-times-selection shape.

STANDS: I could not refute this finding. Nothing at 0b781473 already handles it:
- There is no shortcut comment at view_state.rs L290-313.
- No ledger entry covers it. Ledger 837 is only about the store reads, and it is closed.
- The changelog's "M and Delete on a conversation" entry states no limit for large sets.
- measurements.md rows 684 and 691 time the rule with one conversation only.

The function really does scan every touched conversation for every row on screen: `touched.iter().find(|one| one.is(row))`. `WhoseConversation::is` compares the account id first, a 36-character UUID that is the same for every row of a folder, and then the thread id.

The touched list really can be large, and without any manual selection:
- `conversations_holding` returns one entry per distinct conversation.
- Every message gets a thread id (backfill_thread_ids, threading.rs), so 5,000 one-message conversations give 5,000 touched entries.
- 'Run a rule now' hands `mark_these_read` up to 5,000 messages (running_a_rule_now.rs:119, `.take(MOST_ROWS_WORTH_SELECTING)`), and that calls the catch-up (wx_app.rs:27700, then 12822).
- Undo of a large mark (22323) and a Shift+End selection reach the same code.

In conversation view `s.conversations` holds the whole listing (the plan says so, and the rule was timed over all 22,503 rows). At Pratik's own Inbox size, a 5,000-message rule run gives 22,503 x 5,000 = about 1.1e8 string-pair comparisons. That is roughly half a second to a second with the state lock held on the UI thread, against the project's 100 ms key-press budget. The measured one-conversation cost is 20 ms. At 200,000 messages the cost is several seconds.

The proposed fix is safe:
- `conversations_holding` uses SELECT DISTINCT, and both narrowed listings group by account and conversation, so the (account_id, thread_id) keys are unique. Using `entry().or_insert` keeps the first-match behaviour anyway.
- Checking the touched set before the fresh map keeps `test_a_row_the_change_did_not_touch_is_left_alone` passing, along with the other four unit tests.

One caveat: `mark_these_read` already scans `s.messages` once per message (`iter_mut().find`), and that code is older than 13.2. Fixing this function alone will not make a 5,000-message mark instant. This finding is about the new extra cost only, so it belongs in "should" (real slowness), not "must".

STANDS: I could not refute this finding, and "should" is the right group. At 0b781473, `bring_rows_up_to_date` (view_state.rs:290-313) runs `touched.iter().find(|one| one.is(row))` for every conversation row on screen. In a folder view every row has the same account_id, so each check compares the full account string and then the thread id. The work is rows on screen times conversations touched. It runs inside `lock_state` at wx_app.rs:28106-28110.

`touched` can really be large, through ordinary paths:

The conversation listing has no LIMIT, so `s.conversations` holds every conversation in the folder.

Cost, estimated rather than timed (I could not build), at a few nanoseconds per check:
- At Pratik's real Inbox size, 22,503 rows times 5,000 touched is about 1.1e8 checks, roughly 0.3 to 0.6 s. Today that step takes 15 to 22 ms with one conversation touched (measurements.md:684/691). Nobody has timed it with a selection.
- At a 200,000-message folder with tens of thousands to about 130,000 conversations, it is roughly 1 to 3+ s, with the state lock held on the window's thread.

Nothing marks this as a known limit: no `shortcut:` comment and no ledger entry.

Why "should" and not "must": it is real slowness at the stated load, not wrong results or lost data. Other steps of the same press also cost time (one cache write and one server change per message), but they do not cancel this cost.

The proposed fix is the smallest one that works. `WhoseConversation` already derives Hash. Build one HashSet of the touched (account_id, thread_id) pairs and one HashMap from the `fresh` rows, about six lines. That turns rows × touched into rows + touched. The five existing unit tests still cover the behaviour.

I could not use a binary search on the already-sorted `named` list instead. It would depend on SQLite's sort order matching Rust's, and the unit tests pass the touched list in any order.

findings.title: A mark let go during a check's replay is still sent
findings.what_this_is: The check's replay sends each waiting read or star change to the server. Before each send it asks this function which folder numbering (UIDVALIDITY) the change was kept under.
findings.problem: The function answers None in two cases: the row was kept by an older build, or the row is gone. The private function below it can tell these apart, but `.flatten()` loses the difference. The replay reads None as "old row, send it unchecked", so it sends a change that was let go while the replay ran.
findings.concrete_case: Changes are allowed. A check reads the waiting "read" for message R and starts sending the list. While it waits on the server, the person presses M to mark R unread. That push reaches the server, and stop_waiting_for_what_came_before deletes the waiting "read". The replay then reaches R, gets None, and sends "read". The server now says read while the row here says unread. The next check writes "read" here too, and the person's last mark is lost. This is finding #2, in the other order.
findings.fix: Make the public reader return the private Option<Option<u32>> and delete the flattening wrapper. In the replay, skip a change whose row is gone.
findings.if_we_skip: The race is rare and depends on timing, but when it happens the person's newest mark is silently undone at the server and then here. No test covers it.
findings.evidence: git show 0b781473:src/data/message_cache/waiting_flag_changes.rs L189-191 `.flatten()`. L196-210 keep `Option<Option<u32>>`. wx_app.rs:18947 reads the list once, then :18961 reads the numbering per change, with `None => Ok(None)` at :18976. renumbered.rs:136-141: numbering None means no question is asked and the kept uid is sent. wx_app.rs:29731 deletes the row on a direct push's success. That push runs on its own task, and `git grep APushUnderWay` shows that guard is used only for moves and deletes, not flag pushes.
checker_notes: STANDS: The race happens at 0b781473. I walked the code path and nothing stops it. (1) The replay in wx_app.rs reads the waiting list once, at line 18947. A check reaches it from line 32051, on the account's shared session from `the_session_at`. (2) Pressing M calls `mark_these_read` (line 12766). That calls `spawn_server_change`, which runs on its own `spawn_blocking` task with its own cache connection, and nothing defers it during a check. `handed_to_the_move` only covers moves. `one_check_at_a_time` only orders checks against each other. `APushUnderWay` is used only for moves, deletes and emptying the trash. (3) Both tasks get the same `Arc<MailController>`. `set_flag` takes the session for one command at a time, so the push can run between two of the replay's commands. When the push succeeds, line 29731 calls `stop_waiting_for_what_came_before`. The waiting row's time is earlier than the time M was pressed, so the row is deleted. (4) The replay then reaches R. `the_numbering_a_flag_change_was_kept_under` returns `Ok(None)` because `.flatten()` folds "row gone" into "no numbering". The let-else at line 18960 passes, since both results are `Ok`. A numbering of `None` skips the question to the server (line 18979), and `renumbered::what_it_needs` returns `SendItTo(kept uid)`. `the_number_to_offer_it_at` returns that uid, and `set_flag(SEEN, true)` sends "read". `stop_waiting_for_this_change` then deletes nothing. (5) The same check then lists the folders. `the_flags_to_keep` lays only the changes still waiting over what the server said. R's row is gone, so the server's "read" is written here, and the person's unread mark is lost on both sides. The window is wide in the case the feature exists for: several marks kept offline, each sent with its own round trip to the server. The proposed fix closes the wide window, from reading the list to reaching R. A small window stays: between the row check and the replay's own `set_flag`, which still waits for the session (and asks the folder's numbering when one was kept), the push can still slip in. The fix is still worth making. 'should' fits: timing-dependent, no test, but a real wrong result.

STANDS: The race is real at 0b781473, and nothing in the tree covers it.

How it happens:
1. `send_the_flag_changes_that_were_waiting` (wx_app.rs:18947) reads the list of waiting changes once. It then works through them one by one, and each one waits on the server.
2. `spawn_server_change` sends a person's M press on its own blocking task. It does not wait for the account's turn (`one_check_at_a_time` is taken only in `spawn_mail_sync`). `APushUnderWay` guards moves and deletes only. `mark_these_read` only checks `handed_to_the_move`.
3. The two tasks share the account's session, and that session is locked for one command at a time (`require_imap`, mail_controller.rs:445). So the M press can reach the server between two of the replay's commands.
4. On success, wx_app.rs:29731 calls `stop_waiting_for_what_came_before` and deletes the older waiting "read".
5. When the replay reaches R, `the_numbering_a_flag_change_was_kept_under` uses `.flatten()` and answers Ok(None) for the deleted row. With no numbering, `the_number_to_send_to` sends to the kept number unchecked (renumbered.rs `what_it_needs` gives SendItTo), and `set_flag(SEEN, true)` goes out. `stop_waiting_for_this_change` then deletes nothing.
6. The server now says read while the row here says unread. The next folder sync copies "read" back, so the person's newest mark is lost.

Nothing already covers it:
- The doc comment on the public reader names only "not known then" and "kept by an older build".
- The replay's own comment covers only a row that cannot be read (Err).
- 13.2-11's plan and summary cover the opposite order: a newer row kept while the replay waits.
- The changelog entry of 2026-10-15 says a read or star that reaches the server ends any older waiting one, and states no limit for a check that is already running.
- No ledger row in .planning/WINDOWS.md covers it (853 is the field check of the ordinary order, 765 is the moves ordering). No test and no shortcut comment covers it either.

Caveat on the proposed fix:
- It is safe. Only the replay and one unit test use the public reader. Skipping a deleted row is right whether the push let it go or the message is gone.
- It only narrows the race. The row can still be deleted after the numbering is read, while the replay waits on `the_numbering_now` or on the session lock for its own `set_flag`, and the stale value still goes out.
- A complete fix would re-read the kept row just before sending and skip it unless it is still the same change, or make the flag push take the account's turn.

The timing is rare, so this is "should", not "must".

STANDS: The race is real at 0b781473. The check's replay reads the waiting list once (wx_app.rs:18947), then reads each change's numbering just before sending it (:18961). A row that is gone comes back as None after `.flatten()`, the same as a row kept by an older build. With None, renumbered.rs asks the server nothing and the stale value is sent to the kept uid. The direct M or star push runs on its own spawn_blocking thread and uses the same shared session from the_session_at. That session locks once per command (set_flag holds it for SELECT plus STORE), so the push slips in between the replay's commands. When the push succeeds it deletes the older row (:29731). No guard covers flag pushes: APushUnderWay is used only for moves, deletes and trash emptying. After that, set_message_flags treats the server as the authority, so the check's flag pass or the next check copies the stale value back here. The person's newest mark is undone in both places.

Severity: "should" is honest. The bug needs a change already waiting (an earlier push failed because the server could not be reached), a check replaying that list, and the person changing the same message again within the few seconds of round trips the replay takes. At this load that is rare. Folder size does not matter. The harm is one read or star mark silently reverted, with no message content lost. That is not a "must".

The proposed fix is smaller than the problem, so it only narrows the race. Most of the time the replay is holding the session lock for an earlier change's STORE, so that is when a push usually arrives, and it queues on that lock. tokio's Mutex serves waiters in order, so the push gets the lock next. While the push's STORE is in flight, the replay reads R's row, which is still there, so the fix still sees Some(numbering) and sends the stale value right after the push. The push only deletes the row after its STORE returns. So skipping a gone row protects only a change at least two places behind the one in flight when the push arrived.

A small fix that closes the race: one per-account lock, held by send_the_flag_changes_that_were_waiting for its whole loop, and by the direct flag push around its STORE and the delete at :29731. The replay takes a few seconds at most, so the push waits that long, then sends the newest value last. Removing the flatten wrapper can still go in as tidying, but on its own it does not fix the bug.

findings.title: The Google sign-in check compares the From address, not the account that signs in
findings.what_this_is: authorize asks Google which account a browser sign-in belongs to. refuse_anybody_but then refuses the sign-in unless that account matches the address it was given.
findings.problem: Both callers pass account.email, which is the From address. The token is used to sign in as account.username (XOAUTH2 user= in imap.rs:629 and sign_in_for in mail_controller.rs). These two are separate fields in the editor. So a correct sign-in is refused when the From address differs from the Google account. Ledger 869 accepted a refusal for a Workspace alias on the grounds that the person can change the address here, but on this path that changes the From of every message they send.
findings.concrete_case: A Gmail account set up with the address ada@lovelace.dev (Gmail 'Send mail as'), the username ada.lovelace@gmail.com, and imap.gmail.com. The person picks ada.lovelace@gmail.com in the browser. Google answers ada.lovelace@gmail.com, the comparison is with ada@lovelace.dev, and the sign-in is refused with 'choose ada@lovelace.dev in the browser', an account Google cannot offer. Before 13.2-15 this sign-in was kept and worked.
findings.fix: Pass the login rather than the From address: authorize(&account.username), falling back to account.email when username is blank, at wx_account_manager.rs:844 and :3252. The comparison then checks the account the token will actually be used for.
findings.if_we_skip: People whose From address is not their Google login cannot use the browser sign-in at all, and the only way round it changes how their mail is addressed.
findings.evidence: git show 0b781473:src/presentation/wx_account_manager.rs:844 `.block_on(sign_in.authorize(&account.email))` and :3252 `rt.block_on(auth_mgr.authorize(&account.email))`. :1993 `username: w.user_f.get_value()` is its own field, only pre-filled from the email (:2646). mail_controller.rs sign_in_for passes account.username.clone(). imap.rs:629-631 `xoauth2::credential(&self.config.username, token)`. oauth.rs:863-889 refuse_anybody_but compares the_same_google_account(signing_in_as, &signed_in_as). WINDOWS.md ledger 869 covers only the Workspace alias and was closed as 'kept strict'.
checker_notes:
STANDS: The bug happens at 0b781473. Both browser sign-ins pass account.email: run_oauth_flow at wx_account_manager.rs:3252 and sign_in_for_calendars at :844. The editor keeps username in its own field (:1993). It copies the email into username only when detect_provider knows the domain (:2639-2646), so for a lovelace.dev address the person types ada.lovelace@gmail.com by hand. Account::validate accepts that, as long as username is not blank.

Walking the concrete case:
1. WhoRunsTheMail::of looks at the incoming server first, so imap.gmail.com places the account with Gmail.
2. a_server_its_provider_does_not_run finds nothing wrong, because imap.gmail.com and smtp.gmail.com are both Google's.
3. authorize("ada@lovelace.dev") runs the token exchange, then refuse_anybody_but asks Google for the primary calendar's id. For a consumer Gmail account that id is ada.lovelace@gmail.com.
4. the_same_google_account compares "ada@lovelace.dev" with "adalovelace@gmail.com" and returns false. The error comes back before store_tokens, so nothing is kept.
5. The person is told to choose ada@lovelace.dev in the browser, which Google cannot offer.
6. The next mail check fails in mail_auth::for_account with "needs to sign in again".

Mail would have worked with that token: imap.rs:631 and smtp.rs:627 use config.username, which is ada.lovelace@gmail.com. At 2a4679a9, authorize() took no address and kept the token, so this is a regression from 13.2-15.

Ledger 869 does not cover this. It is about a Workspace account typed under one of its own aliases, and it was kept strict because accepting any address in the organisation would accept a colleague. Comparing against username loosens nothing. It checks the identity the token is actually used for, on both the mail and the separate calendar sign-in.

Why "should" and not "must": the app's documented way to send as another address is to add it under Other addresses (USER_GUIDE.md around line 1683, ALPHA_TESTING.md:397-406) and keep the Gmail address as the account's own. So a supported workaround exists. Only accounts that put the Send mail as address in the account's own address box are hit.

STANDS: The finding holds at 0b781473. Both callers pass account.email to authorize (wx_account_manager.rs:844 and :3252). That value is used as the login_hint and as the address the Google check compares against (oauth.rs refuse_anybody_but calls the_same_google_account). Mail, however, signs in with account.username: XOAUTH2 in imap.rs:631, smtp.rs:627 and mail_controller sign_in_for. Account.username is its own field and validate() requires it. The editor copies the email into it only when detect_provider knows the domain.

Here is the case that fails. An account has email ada@lovelace.dev, username ada.lovelace@gmail.com and server imap.gmail.com. WhoRunsTheMail::of picks Gmail from the server, so the Google check runs. Google answers ada.lovelace@gmail.com and the check compares that with ada@lovelace.dev, so the right sign-in is refused. The refusal tells the person to "choose ada@lovelace.dev in the browser", which is not a Google account. Before 13.2-15 (commit 57bc9cb0) there was no check at all.

None of the project's existing notes covers this:
- Ledger 869 and the changelog only cover a Workspace account typed under one of its own Google aliases, closed as "kept strict". The reason given there, that accepting any address of the organisation would accept a colleague, does not apply to comparing against the login field.
- No ledger entry, "shortcut:" comment or test mentions username against email for a Google sign-in.

Two corrections to the finding:
1. "if_we_skip" overstates the harm. Other Addresses to Send From (Alt+O, identities.rs) lets the person set the email to the Gmail login and keep ada@lovelace.dev as an address to send from. Replies to mail sent to that address pick it automatically. Only the default From for new mail changes.
2. The fix as written is incomplete. who_holds_the_calendars.rs uses account.email in two places that name the address to choose in the browser: what_sign_in_again_says_as_it_begins (:459) and SignsIn { address: account.email } (:408). Both must switch to the same field, or the spoken address and the login_hint will disagree with the check. test_sign_in_again_names_the_address_to_choose_in_the_browser may need its fixture checked.

The username fallback is not needed, because validate() already refuses an empty username. "should" is still the right group: a correct sign-in is refused for a less common setup, but there is a workaround.

STANDS: I could not refute it. The bug happens at 0b781473. Both callers in wx_account_manager.rs (lines 844 and 3252) call authorize(&account.email). refuse_anybody_but then compares Google's answer, the id of the primary calendar, with that address. The token is used under account.username in two places: XOAUTH2 in imap.rs:631, and Credentials::new(self.config.username, token) in smtp.rs. XOAUTH2 is the login method that sends a token instead of a password. The editor keeps Username as its own field and fills it from the address only when detect_provider knows the domain, which it does not for ada@lovelace.dev. WhoRunsTheMail::of places the account with Gmail by its server, imap.gmail.com, so the browser sign-in runs and is refused. The refusal then says "choose ada@lovelace.dev in the browser", which Google cannot offer. Before 13.2-15, authorize() took no address and kept this sign-in. Google ends unverified sign-ins weekly, so a working account of this kind hits the refusal within days at the next Sign In Again. The Calendars, Contacts and Tasks sign-in is hit the same way.

Ledger 869 and the changelog limit cover only "a Google Workspace account entered under one of its other addresses". The closing decision, "kept strict", was about not accepting any address of the organisation. Comparing with the username is just as strict: it is the one account the token is used for.

Two parts of the finding are overstated, and the fix is a little short.
1. "Cannot use the browser sign-in at all" and "the only way round it changes how their mail is addressed" are not quite true. The app has Other Addresses to Send From (Alt+O). The person can make the Gmail login the account's address and keep the alias as another From address, and replies to mail sent to the alias go out from it automatically. Only new messages would start from the Gmail address.
2. The smallest correct fix also has to change the sentence spoken when sign-in starts. It reads account.email in who_holds_the_calendars.rs, at line 459 (what_sign_in_again_says_as_it_begins) and line 408 (the separate sign-in's address). Without that change, the person is still told to choose the alias. One small helper, the username or the address when the username is blank, used at all four places, fixes it.

Group: "should" is honest, not "must". It is a regression, but only in one narrow setup (a Gmail account whose address is set to a send-as address on another domain). It has a workaround, and it loses no data and opens no security hole. The owner has already accepted a refusal like this for the Workspace case. Load does not matter here.

findings.title: Unticking Calendar in Google's consent screen now refuses the mail sign-in
findings.what_this_is: refuse_anybody_but learns who signed in by asking the Google Calendar API for the primary calendar (google_api.rs:814 the_address_signed_in).
findings.problem: Google's consent screen gives a separate tick box for each permission when an app asks for several. The 'gmail' sign-in asks for mail, contacts, calendar and tasks. A token granted without calendar gets 403 from the calendar call, and the whole sign-in is refused with 'Google did not say which account signed in', even though mail would work. The changelog says the Calendar API must be enabled for the key, but says nothing about a person unticking it.
findings.concrete_case: A person who wants only mail unticks 'See, edit, share calendars' and keeps mail. The code exchange succeeds, the calendar call returns 403, the error is mapped to 'Google did not say which account signed in, so the sign-in was not kept. Try again', and no token is stored. They try again, untick it again, and are refused again. Before 13.2-15 the mail token was kept.
findings.fix: Find out who signed in through a permission the consent screen cannot untick: add the `email` scope to both Google sign-ins and read the address from https://openidconnect.googleapis.com/v1/userinfo. Or, when tokens.scope lacks calendar, ask Gmail's users/me/profile on the mail sign-in.
findings.if_we_skip: A reasonable privacy choice on Google's own screen blocks the person's mail, and the message points them at the wrong cause.
findings.evidence: git show 0b781473:src/service/oauth.rs L89-106 'gmail' default_scopes: mail.google.com, contacts, calendar, tasks. L863-889 refuse_anybody_but: google.the_address_signed_in(&tokens.access_token).await.map_err(.. 'Google did not say which account signed in, so the sign-in was not kept' ..)?. google_api.rs:814-824 the_address_signed_in GETs {calendar_base}/calendars/primary. docs/changelog.md:1826-1842 mentions the Calendar API requirement and no partial consent.
checker_notes:
STANDS: The finding holds at 0b781473. A Gmail account with "sign in through the browser" ticked for mail (use_oauth) goes through run_oauth_flow, wx_account_manager.rs:3217, which uses provider_of, so the provider is "gmail". That calls AuthManager::authorize, oauth.rs:795. The code exchange succeeds at step 4. Then refuse_anybody_but at L863 has no early return for Google. It calls GoogleApiClient::the_address_signed_in, google_api.rs:814, which GETs {calendar_base}/calendars/primary. A token whose calendar permission was unticked gets a 403, Google's "insufficient scopes" refusal. That error is mapped at L875-879 to "Google did not say which account signed in, so the sign-in was not kept", and the `?` returns before store_tokens at L845. Nothing is stored, so mail cannot sign in.

Nothing in the head code checks or tolerates a partial grant: tokens.scope is never read in authorize. At 2a4679a9, authorize went straight from the exchange to store_tokens, so the mail-only token was kept and mail worked. That makes this a regression from 13.2-15 (57bc9cb0).

The browser mail sign-in for Gmail is a documented, supported path. PROVIDER_SETUP.md:21 says such an account needs nothing more. The docs and changelog do not mention unticking a permission. PROVIDER_SETUP.md:537-538 tells the person only to check that the Calendar API is turned on, which is the wrong cause here. So the misleading advice in the finding is also accurate. Google's granular consent screen lets a person untick any non-sign-in scope, calendar included, so the trigger is a real situation. The same refusal also hits the separate calendars sign-in when only calendar is unticked, but the finding's mail case alone reproduces.

STANDS: Nothing at 0b781473 handles this. `refuse_anybody_but` (oauth.rs:863-889) is new in 13.2-15 (57bc9cb0; it is not in 2a4679a9). It runs for both Google sign-ins: the "gmail" mail sign-in and the separate calendars, contacts and tasks sign-in. It always learns who signed in from `GoogleApiClient::the_address_signed_in`, which GETs calendars/primary (google_api.rs:814). Any error from that call becomes "Google did not say which account signed in, so the sign-in was not kept", and `store_tokens` never runs.

Nothing in oauth.rs reads `tokens.scope`. It contains no check for a missing permission and no fallback to another way of learning the address. The tests near L2383 and L2433 cover a wrong account and a failed lookup, but no token that lacks the calendar permission.

The ledger (WINDOWS.md 865-869) covers the Microsoft check, the wrong-account and right-account runs, and Workspace aliases. It says nothing about partial consent. The changelog and PROVIDER_SETUP.md:537-538 send this error to "check the Google Calendar API is turned on", which is the wrong cause here. Step 6 of the setup page says "Allow them" for the calendars, contacts and tasks sign-in only. It does not cover the mail sign-in, which is documented as an option (PROVIDER_SETUP.md:236).

Google's granular-permissions page, last updated 2026-05-26, says that when an app asks for more than one non-sign-in permission, people can choose which ones to approve. Apps must not assume they got all of them. A desktop-client write-up (jpassing.com, 2022) reports per-permission tick boxes, some unticked by default. So a token without the calendar permission is a realistic case. The calendar call then answers 403 for insufficient permissions, and the sign-in is refused. Before 13.2-15 the token was kept and mail worked.

The same refusal hits the calendars, contacts and tasks sign-in: unticking only calendar now also blocks contacts and tasks.

The proposed fix does not break anything. `openid` and `email` are sign-in permissions, which Google's page says always come as one approve-or-deny (no tick box), so the userinfo address is always there. Adding `email` is non-sensitive and is a one-time new consent for each sign-in.

Group "should" is right: the mail browser sign-in is not Gmail's default path (the app password is), but this is a real regression with a misleading error message.

STANDS: I could not refute it, so the finding stands. At 0b781473, `authorize` (oauth.rs L834-840) calls `refuse_anybody_but` before `store_tokens`. For both Google sign-ins, that function asks `the_address_signed_in`, which reads `/calendars/primary` (google_api.rs L814-816). Any error there becomes "Google did not say which account signed in, so the sign-in was not kept" (L872-880), and nothing is stored. No code checks `tokens.scope` first. The 'gmail' provider asks for mail, contacts, calendar and tasks (L94-107). It is still reachable: `run_oauth_flow` (wx_account_manager.rs L3217-3252) uses `provider_of`, which returns "gmail" for Gmail and Workspace accounts set to sign in through a browser. The separate sign-in for calendars, contacts and tasks (L827-845) goes through the same check.

Google's consent screen shows a tick box for each permission when an app asks for more than one, and only the sign-in permissions (openid, email, profile) are always granted. Google's granular-permissions guide says this, and jpassing.com's 2022 write-up on IAP Desktop shows it happening in a desktop app. So a person who leaves Calendar unticked gets a working token, and the calendar call is then refused. The result: their mail sign-in (or their contacts-and-tasks sign-in) is thrown away, with a message that names the wrong cause.

This is a 13.2 regression: commits 722b3ba0 and 57bc9cb0 (13.2-15). Before them the token was kept. Nothing in the changelog, the planning files or the code mentions people leaving a permission unticked, and no test covers a token without the calendar permission.

On the group, I agree with "should". It does not depend on load and loses no data. It only happens when someone unticks Calendar, and ticking it works around it. But the misleading message makes that workaround hard to find, so it is more than "nice".

The proposed fix is the smallest one that works for both sign-ins. Add the `email` scope to both Google provider lists, which cannot be unticked, and read the address from Google's userinfo endpoint in `the_address_signed_in` instead of the calendar. That is one URL and one scope string per list. A Gmail-profile fallback would only help the mail sign-in and would add a second code path.

findings.title: A rule's move now costs four server round trips instead of one
findings.what_this_is: carry_out_the_moves sends each rule's move to the server. Since 13.2-08 it then asks the destination where the message landed (settle_a_moved_row).
findings.problem: The settle opens (SELECTs) the destination folder and searches it, and the next message's move then has to SELECT the source folder again. Each filed message goes from 1 command to 4, and 2 of the new ones are full folder opens, which are slow on a large Inbox.
findings.concrete_case: After a week away, 800 messages arrive and a mailing-list rule files 400 of them. Before: 400 UID MOVE commands. Now: 400 × (UID MOVE, SELECT List, UID SEARCH, SELECT INBOX), which is 1,200 extra commands, 800 of them opening the folders again. At 0.1 to 0.5 s each, the check runs several minutes longer.
findings.fix: Collect (row, destination) in the loop and settle after it, grouped by destination, so the source is opened once and each destination once.
findings.if_we_skip: Checks after a big arrival get slow exactly when there is the most to sort, and the owner has already reported slowness in M and Delete.
findings.evidence: git show 0b781473:src/application/mail_sync.rs L1352-1418: in the loop, controller.move_message(&from.path, ..) and then settle_a_moved_row(controller, cache, moving.message_row, &account_id, &into.path). moves_waiting.rs:1031 where_it_is(destination, ..) leads to mail_controller.rs:741-748 uids_with_message_id, which SELECTs when selected_folder() != folder. mail_controller.rs:711-718 move_message SELECTs `from` again under the same rule. git diff 2a4679a9 0b781473 shows that the settle call is new in this range.
checker_notes:
STANDS: The slowdown is real at 0b781473. carry_out_the_moves (mail_sync.rs:1356-1418) calls controller.move_message(&from.path, ..). That is MailController::move_message (mail_controller.rs:711-718), which sends SELECT for the source folder only if the session does not already have it open, then sends UID MOVE. After a successful move and cache move, the loop now calls settle_a_moved_row (moves_waiting.rs:1013-1043, new in this range per git diff). That calls where_it_is, which is uids_with_message_id (mail_controller.rs:741-748): it SELECTs the destination because the open folder is still the source, then sends UID SEARCH HEADER MESSAGE-ID. ImapSession::select_folder (imap.rs:1149) records the destination as the open folder, so on the next message move_message sees the wrong folder open and SELECTs the source again.

Nothing on this path avoids the extra commands. Moves and searches pass the same may_change gate, the settle runs on every Moved::Moved, the destination's UID is never read from the MOVE answer (COPYUID) instead of searched for, and no shortcut: or ponytail: comment names the cost. Before the change the source stayed open from fetch_headers, so each filed message cost one UID MOVE. Now it costs SELECT source, UID MOVE, SELECT destination and UID SEARCH: 3 extra round trips per message, 2 of them folder opens.

The 13.2 change to uids_to_fetch makes the concrete case reachable. It now takes every arrived uid with no 500 cap, so a week's 800 arrivals all go through the rules in one check. The audit's corrected_fix (audit-2026-10-14-findings.json:200) expected only one destination SELECT followed by one SELECT of the source at the later flag read. It did not account for the source being reopened inside the loop, so this cost is not a stated limitation either.

400 filed messages therefore cost about 1,200 extra commands, 800 of them folder opens. That is minutes on a background check, not a correctness or data-loss problem, so "should" (real slowness) fits. The proposed fix holds: collect (row, destination) pairs in the loop, then settle them afterwards grouped by destination.

STANDS: The finding holds at 0b781473, and nothing at the head commit already covers it.

How the loop runs:
1. The session is one connection kept open behind a lock (mail_controller.rs:369-408). It remembers which folder is open in `selected` (imap.rs:1149).
2. `MailController::move_message` (mail_controller.rs:711-718) and `uids_with_message_id` (mail_controller.rs:741-748) each open their folder again whenever a different folder is open. Opening a folder is the IMAP command SELECT.
3. `ReplaysAMove::where_it_is` for MailController is `uids_with_message_id` (moves_waiting.rs:588-590). That runs `UID SEARCH HEADER MESSAGE-ID` (imap.rs:1522-1527).
4. Inside `carry_out_the_moves` (mail_sync.rs:1338-1418), every moved message now goes through `settle_a_moved_row` (moves_waiting.rs:1013-1043). That opens the destination and searches it. The next message's move then finds the destination open and opens the source again.

So each filed message after the first costs four commands: SELECT source, UID MOVE, SELECT destination, UID SEARCH. Before, it cost one, the UID MOVE. `git log -S` shows the settle call arrived in fb694c7b (13.2-08), inside the range.

The same plan also removed the 500-message cap, so one check can now run the rules over every arrival after a week away. That makes the 400-message case realistic.

Already handled? No:
- There is no `shortcut:` or `ponytail:` comment in mail_sync.rs, moves_waiting.rs or mail_controller.rs.
- The 13.2-08 plan and summary talk about batching only for the arrival fetch (T-13.2-17), never for the settle.
- The changelog entry (changelog.md:1925-1937) gives the fix and says nothing about its cost.
- The nearest ledger entry, 850, only says "how long one check takes over thousands of arrivals has not been timed". It does not name the extra SELECT and SEARCH for each moved message.
- No test counts commands on this path.

Does the proposed fix break anything? I checked whether waiting to settle until after the loop changes the result, and it does not:
- `settle_a_moved_row` reads only the row, the account and the destination.
- Two rows with the same Message-ID filed into one folder end up the same way: both are let go and the next read of the destination brings each one once.
- The steps after the moves (`carry_out_the_deletes` and the flag read) work on the source folder and do not touch the moved rows.
- The only cost is that the moved row keeps its reserved number until the loop ends, instead of for one round trip.

Group: the code is correct but slow at the expected load, so this is "should".

STANDS: The extra commands are real at 0b781473, but "should" overstates them and the fix has a cost the finding leaves out.

What happens: each filed message now costs 4 IMAP commands instead of 1 (3 for the first message). Those are UID MOVE, then SELECT of the destination and UID SEARCH HEADER MESSAGE-ID inside settle_a_moved_row, then a SELECT of the source again for the next move. SELECT opens a folder on the server. Checked in three places: mail_sync.rs L1356-1405, moves_waiting.rs L1029-1031, and mail_controller.rs L711-717 and L741-746, where each command re-selects whenever selected_folder() differs. The settle was added by fb694c7b (13.2-08) to fix duplicate rows (#10).

The 400-message case is possible. uids_to_fetch fetches everything newer than the newest held message, with no limit, so 800 arrivals are all fetched in one check and the rules can file 400 of them.

Why it does not reach "should" at the expected load:
1. **Bounded cost.** The extra work grows in a straight line, 3 commands per filed message, and runs in a background check.
2. **Common case is small.** A check that files a few messages gains about a second.
3. **UI keeps moving.** The sync shares one session per account with the UI (mail_session.rs), but the lock is taken per command and tokio's Mutex serves waiters in order. A user's M or Delete during the burst waits for at most one sync command plus perhaps one SELECT. It does not wait for the whole check.
4. **Overstated SELECT cost.** "Full folder opens, slow on a large Inbox" overstates it. SELECT (CONDSTORE) is one round trip that returns a few status lines, not the folder's contents.
5. **Unrelated complaint.** The link to the owner's M/Delete slowness is a different mechanism (acting on a conversation).

So this is a rare background burst that runs about 3 to 4 times longer, with no wrong result. That is "nice", not "should".

The fix is not free. Moving every settle after the loop cuts the 2N SELECTs to about D+1, where D is the number of destinations. The UID SEARCHes stay, so the extra cost roughly halves, not more. It also stretches the time between cache.move_message and the settle from one round trip to the whole loop, which is minutes in the 400-message case. the_server_holds_it_at runs an UPDATE that sets folder_id to the destination without checking where the row is now. So if the user deletes or moves a just-filed message during that window, the settle can quietly put it back.

A safer fix of about the same size groups by destination and finishes one group at a time. For each group: do its MOVEs (source selected once), then cache.move_message for each, then SELECT the destination once and settle the group. That is about 2N+2D commands, and the window stays as long as one group.

findings.title: A day deleted in one calendar changes the same meeting in another
findings.what_this_is: When a feed or calendar-server read meets a moved or cancelled day, this fold first asks whether somebody deleted that day here. If so, it now calls the day off this calendar's series.
findings.problem: The "deleted here" set comes from events_deleted_here, which holds every deletion note of the whole account, not just this calendar's. 13.2-31.6 scoped the fold's lookups and deletes to one calendar but left this check account-wide. Since 13.2, a hit also writes to this calendar's series. So a deletion in calendar A changes calendar B: the cross-calendar reach the phase set out to remove.
findings.concrete_case: Account has two feeds, the class feed and the school feed, and both carry the weekly assembly with Tuesday 10 March moved to 14:00. The person deletes the moved day in the class feed, which writes a note for "assembly:2026-03-10T09:00:00Z". At the next school-feed refresh, deleted_here.holds(compound) is true. The school series gets 10 March called off and returns early, so the school's moved day is never written (if new) or never updated again (if held). The school calendar shows no assembly that day, or a stale time. A feed's note is never sent, so it is never let go, and this lasts for good. With two server calendars it lasts until a week after the note is taken, and an edit to B's series sends that EXDATE to B's server (EXDATE is in PROPERTIES_A_CHANGE_REPLACES).
findings.fix: For the two CalDAV reads (sync_caldav_calendar and refresh_subscription), build the set for the calendar being read. Pass the calendar id to events_deleted_here and keep only notes whose calendar_id matches; deleted_calendar_events already stores it. Keep the account-wide set for Google if that decision stands. Add the reverse of test_a_feeds_moved_day_deleted_here_leaves_a_meeting_in_another_calendar_as_it_was: delete in the other calendar, refresh the feed, and check the feed's day is untouched.
findings.if_we_skip: Deleting a meeting day in one calendar silently hides or freezes it in another calendar that still holds it.
findings.evidence: git diff 2a4679a9 0b781473 -- src/application/caldav_sync.rs: old code `if deleted_here.holds(&compound_id) || deleted_here.holds(&changed.uid) { return Ok(()); }`. New code at 0b781473 L1070-1079 calls `with_one_more_day_called_off(&series, ..)` and `save_calendar_event(&after)`. The feed refresh calls the fold since e5d8516d (L1289-1305). git show 0b781473:src/application/calendar.rs L529-553: "Not narrowed to one calendar, deliberately", built from `cache.deleted_calendar_events(account_id)`. src/data/message_cache/calendar.rs L1042-1060: delete_calendar_event writes the note with calendar_id and the compound provider_event_id. caldav_sync.rs L127-138: a read-only calendar's push returns early, so its notes are never taken. wx_app.rs L32964-33016: feeds, server calendars, Google and Outlook all sync under the same account id `aid`. 13.2-31.6's own doc at caldav_sync.rs L1032-1039 says two calendars may carry the same meeting, each its own copy.
checker_notes:
REFUTED: I followed the code path at 0b781473, and the only real effect is one the project already records as a known gap.

1. The series write is not new harm. When the deleted-here check hits, the fold calls with_one_more_day_called_off on the series of the calendar being read and keeps its pending flag as it was. On a normal pass, one_day_kept_out_of_the_series (calendar.rs L2869-2881) makes the same write with TheProviderItself: the day is called off and pending stays the series' own. So B's series ends up the same whether or not A holds a deletion note. The day really was moved in B's own data, so calling it off is correct either way. The EXDATE point fails for the same reason: B's series carries that EXDATE on a normal pass too.

2. The real difference is smaller. While A's note stands, B's own moved-day row is not written or updated. If B already holds it, it stays as it was; if it is new, it is not stored. The cause is that events_deleted_here asks across the whole account, and that is a written, recorded decision:
- The code says "Not narrowed to one calendar, deliberately" (calendar.rs L529-531).
- Ledger 825 is open (.planning/WINDOWS.md L842). It says "the read of the other calendar leaves that calendar's copy as it was for as long as the note is kept, rather than updating it ... not brought up to date until the note is let go". It closes "when a deletion note is asked within its calendar", which is exactly the proposed fix.
- 13.2-31.6-PLAN section 5 names this function and says "Ledger 825 already carries narrowing it, and this plan leaves it there". Its claim that the check "never reaches another calendar's row" holds: on a hit, B's read writes only B's rows.

3. It is not a 13.2 regression for server calendars. At 2a4679a9 the fold already returned early on the same account-wide hit (`if deleted_here.holds(&compound_id) || deleted_here.holds(&changed.uid) { return Ok(()); }`), so B's moved day was not written then either.

What remains is the gap ledger 825 already describes, so by the review rules it is not a new finding. One fair note for the ledger: its "until the note is let go" understates feeds. Nothing ever marks a feed's note as taken (the push for read-only calendars returns early), so for a feed the gap never closes. That is a correction to the ledger text, not a new bug.

STANDS: The wrong result does happen at 0b781473, and nothing covers it.

How it happens:
- events_deleted_here (calendar.rs L532) builds its set from cache.deleted_calendar_events(account_id), which reads every note of the account and drops calendar_id. Every note stores calendar_id (message_cache/calendar.rs L1046-1058).
- sync_caldav_calendar (L807) and refresh_subscription (L1225) both pass that one set to one_caldav_day_kept_out_of_its_series.
- In the fold, deleted_here.holds(&compound_id) (L1063) calls the day off the reading calendar's own series and returns before the day's row is written. seen_uids gets the compound id at the top of the fold, so a row already held stays, but it is never updated again.
- Feeds, server calendars, Google and Outlook all sync under the same account id (wx_app.rs L32964-33016). The table allows one UID in two calendars: UNIQUE(account_id, calendar_id, provider_event_id).
- A feed's note is never sent, so it is never taken. let_go_of_deletions_taken_before only deletes rows where taken_at IS NOT NULL. So a note from a feed masks the other calendar for good.

Concrete case: calendar B first sees a moved day after the person deleted the same day (same UID and RECURRENCE-ID) in calendar A. B never stores the moved day, and B's series has that date called off. B shows nothing on that day.

Why it is not already handled:
- Ledger 825 (open, todo, phase 14) names the account-wide set and the right closing condition ("a deletion note is asked within its calendar"). But it describes only two Google calendars, and it says the other copy is "left as it was" and "nothing is lost". For the CalDAV and feed fold that is not true: B's series is written to, and a new day is never stored.
- The 13.2-31.6 changelog entry (docs/changelog.md L1523-1525) promises that two calendars carrying the same meeting "each now keeps its own". Ledger 904 marks the fold's cross-calendar reach as fixed.
- The comment "Not narrowed to one calendar, deliberately" rests on the idea that a provider id names one event. The fold's own 13.2-31.6 doc (L1032-1039) says the opposite.
- test_a_feeds_moved_day_deleted_here_leaves_a_meeting_in_another_calendar_as_it_was only checks the other direction.

Where the finding overstates:
- For a day B already holds, the freeze predates 13.2. The old code also returned early (since ad2b0fd3 for server calendars). The 13.2-19 call-off is actually the right shape there: the whole-event loop has just rewritten B's series without the EXDATE (carry_over_local_only does not keep exception_dates), so without it B would show the day twice.
- The claim that an edit pushes the EXDATE to B's server is not special to this bug. A normal fold of a held moved day leaves the same EXDATE on the series (the a_meeting_held_in_another_calendar helper says that is "the shape a read leaves").
- What is new in 13.2 is the hidden day, and the whole path for feeds (the feed refresh has called the fold only since e5d8516d).

Is the proposed fix safe? Yes. Narrowing the set to the calendar being read would also stop a pre-existing false mask. When an event moves between calendars, owe_a_deletion_from_the_calendar_it_left writes a note under the same UID for the calendar it left, and the account-wide set then hides the event in its new calendar too. One condition: a note with no calendar_id should still count as a match, so old notes keep masking.

Why "should" and not "must": the trigger is narrow (one UID in two calendars of one account, plus a deleted moved day), the server copy is untouched, and the root cause predates 13.2 and is partly ledgered.

STANDS: The mechanism checks out at 0b781473, so the finding stands. Each step:
- `events_deleted_here` (calendar.rs L532-553) reads every deletion note in the account.
- Both reads use it: `refresh_subscription` at caldav_sync.rs L1225 and `sync_caldav_calendar` at L808.
- `delete_calendar_event` (message_cache/calendar.rs L1042-1060) writes the note under the row's `provider_event_id`. For a moved day that is the compound name `uid:recurrence-id`, set by the fold at L1158.
- When the fold finds that name in the set (L1070-1079), it reads the series of the calendar being read, calls the day off it, saves it and returns.
- A feed's note never goes away. A feed is never pushed (L127-138 also skips read-only calendars). `forget_deleted_calendar_event` refuses any note that carries a provider's name.

So when calendar A's note matches a day in calendar B, B's series loses that day and B's moved-day row is never written or updated again. For a feed this lasts for good. The direction the phase tested (A's own refresh) is safe; this reverse direction has no test.

The group should be "should", not "must":
1. **Common sequence.** Both calendars usually hold the moved day before anyone deletes it. Then B's series already has the day called off from its normal fold, and the only effect is that B's copy stops being updated. That is the effect open ledger 825 already describes, and it predates 13.2: before the phase, a CalDAV read that found a note returned early in the same way.
2. **The hidden-day case is narrow.** B shows nothing that day only if B first meets the moved day after the deletion (subscribed later, or the publisher adds it later), or if the publisher moves it again. For a CalDAV calendar, 13.2 changes "B shows the day at its old time" into "B hides the day": a different wrong result, not a new one.
3. **Not a regression for feeds.** Before 13.2-19 feeds did not keep moved days apart from their series at all, so a deletion noted the plain UID and hid B's whole series.
4. **No data is lost.** No server and no typed words are touched. Only a second calendar's view of a meeting is hidden or frozen.
5. **Deferred on purpose, but for a wrong reason.** Plan 13.2-31.6, premise 5, kept the account-wide set and pointed at ledger 825. Its reason was that asking the set "can only stop a read writing", which has been false since 13.2-19, when a match started writing the called-off day to the series. Ledger 825 is also Google-only and says "nothing is lost… until the note is let go", which is wrong for feed notes, since they are never let go. Because the ledger is wrong, this is still a finding and not a known limitation.

The fix is the smallest that works, and it matches ledger 825's own closing condition: build the set for the two CalDAV reads only from notes whose `calendar_id` is the calendar being read, and add the reverse test (delete in one calendar, refresh the other). The same change also stops the whole-event check at L1256 and L863 reaching across calendars. Ledger 825's text should be widened to cover feeds and server calendars.

findings.title: A contact edited or deleted while Google creates it is lost or comes back
findings.what_this_is: When a contact typed here has been created at Google or Outlook, the sync saves the whole contact row again with its new identity (the provider's name for it). Since 13.2-17 this runs on every sync, not only on the rare full read.
findings.problem: The row it saves is the copy read before the network call (`here.into_contacts()`, read even before the merge loop). Whatever the person did to that contact in the meantime is written over, and `told` clears the waiting flag. 13.2-20 fixed exactly this race for tasks (rename_task) and notes (a_backend_took_the_note); contacts were left out.
findings.concrete_case: Someone adds "Ann", presses F5, then opens Ann and adds her phone number while createContact is still in flight. write_down saves the old copy of Ann with pending false. The phone number is gone here and never reaches Google. If they delete Ann in that second instead, delete_contact writes no deletion note, because she had no identity yet, and write_down puts her back. She is now on screen again and also at Google.
findings.fix: Settle the create the way rename_task does. Inside one transaction, read the row again by id. If it is gone, record a deletion for the new Google or Outlook identity. If it changed since the snapshot, add only the identity and keep pending set. If it is unchanged, save as today. The CardDAV made-here PUT (carddav_sync.rs L337-355) and the change pushes' `write_down(contact.told(..))` have the same shape and can share the helper.
findings.if_we_skip: On the most common sync path, an edit made just after a sync starts disappears without a word, and a contact the person deleted comes back.
findings.evidence: `git show 78bd443c -- src/application/contacts_sync.rs` (13.2-17) removes `if read_the_whole_address_book {` around the Google create push and `if delta_link.is_none() {` around the Outlook one. At 0b781473: L2725 `let locals = here.into_contacts();`, L2736 `google.create_contact(token, &person).await`, L2739-2761 build `local.also_known_to(..).told(..)` from the snapshot and call `write_down(cache, &updated, ..)`. L2041-2048 write_down is a plain save_contact. data/message_cache/mod.rs L927-948: `told` sets `pending` from the identities alone. data/message_cache/contacts.rs L1080-1099: delete_contact copies deleted_contacts rows only from contact_identities. The premises of .planning/phases/13.2-the-audit-s-fixes/13.2-20-PLAN.md cover tasks, notes and events (13.2-20.1), not contacts, and `.planning/WINDOWS.md` has no ledger row for it.
checker_notes:
STANDS: The bug is real at 0b781473. I followed the code step by step and found nothing that stops it.

1. A contact typed here gets pending=true, no identities, and source "local" (contact_convert.rs L315-356). That passes the create filter at contacts_sync.rs L2731.
2. The sync runs on its own thread with its own copy of the store (wx_app.rs L32464-32484). It holds no lock or transaction across the network wait. ASyncUnderWay only blocks undo, so the interface can still save or delete contacts during a sync.
3. Google: the snapshot is read at L2594, after list_contacts. The create pass reuses it through `here.into_contacts()` at L2725 and never reads the row again. After `create_contact(..).await` (L2736), it builds the row from the old copy plus `.told(..)` and saves it with write_down. write_down is a plain save_contact (L2041-2048).
4. save_contact is an upsert, meaning it inserts the row if missing and overwrites it if present (contacts.rs L128-166). It also replaces the identities. `told` sets pending only from the identities (mod.rs L944-946), so pending becomes false.
5. Edit case: the editor saves the phone number with pending=true between the snapshot and write_down. write_down then overwrites it with the old copy and pending=false. The phone number is gone here, and no later sync sends it to Google.
6. Delete case: the panel's Delete (managers.rs L3230) calls delete_contact. That writes deletion notes only from contact_identities (contacts.rs L1085-1093), and Ann has none yet, so no note is written. write_down then puts her back with a Google identity. On the next sync her etag matches what is stored, so nothing moves her again. She stays here and at Google.
7. Outlook does the same at L2968-2998.

Nothing in the module guards this. Its own comment (L998-1001) says a contact must be read again by id so that "an edit made here while the sync runs" is kept. That re-read is done for the merge loop but not here. There is no test and no ledger row for it. 13.2-20 closed this exact race for tasks and notes, and 13.2-20.1 for events, under audit #17. Contacts were not listed in that finding. 13.2-17 (78bd443c) made this path run on every sync, where before it ran only on a full read, which for Google was in practice the first sync.

The window is wider than the reviewer's one-contact case suggests. A vCard import marks new contacts pending with no identities (contacts.rs L835-841). The next sync creates them one network call at a time, all from that one old snapshot. Any edit or delete of a not-yet-sent imported contact made in the next minute or two is undone without a word.

For a single typed contact the timing is narrow: contacts sync only when the person starts it. The project's own audit put this same race for tasks and notes under "Should fix", so I suggest "should" rather than "must".

STANDS: The bug is real at 0b781473, and nothing in the code, tests, changelog or ledger covers it.

How it happens:
- The sync runs on its own thread with its own database connection (wx_app.rs:32464-32484). Nothing stops the person from deleting a contact from the Contacts list, or saving an edit in the contact manager, while it runs. The only guard, ASyncUnderWay, covers undo and nothing else.
- Both create passes work from a copy of the contacts read before the network calls start: Google `let locals = here.into_contacts()` at L2725, Outlook at L2968. They never read a contact again before or after `create_contact(..).await`.
- After each create, `write_down` (L2041-2048) saves that old copy in full. `save_contact` (contacts.rs:128-205) overwrites every column. `told` (mod.rs:927-948) works out `pending` from the identities alone, so it comes out false.
- `delete_contact` (contacts.rs:1080-1099) writes a deletion note only from `contact_identities`. A contact with no identity yet gets none, and `write_down` then puts the row back.

A long window is realistic. Imported vCard contacts are left pending with no identity (contacts.rs:835-842, `waiting_to_be_sent`). Since 13.2-17 (78bd443c) every sync creates them one network call at a time, so with a few hundred imported contacts the pass can run for minutes. If the person deletes a duplicate during the pass, it reappears here and is also created at Google. If they fix a phone number, the fix is lost here and never sent.

Why it is not already covered:
- No test exists for it. The two tests at L13268 and L13300 cover only the merge loop's re-read by id.
- No ledger row in .planning/WINDOWS.md mentions it.
- 13.2-21 (shape note 6) says the create passes read the old copy only so that a contact made during the loop goes out at the next sync. It does not name losing an edit or bringing back a deleted contact.
- Audit #1 and 13.2-20 / 20.1 fixed this same race for tasks, notes and events only.
- The changelog entry at line 1685 says "an edit made while the sync runs is still kept" for contact syncs. That is wrong for the create pass.

The proposed fix is sound. It is what rename_task already does: read the row again by id, record a deletion if it is gone, otherwise add only the new identity. One detail it must not miss: when the contact changed during the call, the new identity also needs change_is_waiting set to true. Otherwise changes_waiting_for will never send the edit.

Group: "should", not "must". The project's own verdict on the identical race (audit #1) chose "should" because it needs an edit to the same item while a push is running.

STANDS: The race is real at 0b781473, but the example given is not how it happens, and the group should be "should".

What I checked:
- `here` is read (L2594) after `list_contacts` and before the merge loop. `into_contacts()` (L2725 Google, L2968 Outlook) is that copy.
- After `create_contact` returns, `write_down` saves the copy with `told()`, which sets pending to false. `save_contact` replaces the whole row and its identities.
- The sync opens its own MessageCache connection (wx_app.rs L32484), so the window can write in the middle of it.
- `delete_contact` writes a deletion note only from `contact_identities`.
- Nothing in WINDOWS.md covers this, and 13.2-20 and 13.2-20.1 never mention contacts.

So an edit saved between the read and that contact's `write_down` is lost and never sent. A deletion made in that gap is undone: the contact comes back here and also exists at Google.

Why the example is wrong: the only way to edit an existing contact is the Contact Manager. It is a modal dialog (a window that blocks the rest of the program) and saves only when it closes (managers.rs L2841-2853). Pressing F5, then opening it, editing Ann and closing it inside the one network call of a single create is not a real case. The delete variant (Delete, then confirming) is possible but needs about one second of bad luck.

The real case is a bulk import. Imported vCards (wx_app.rs L2751, L2766, L19522) are saved as waiting to be sent. Since 13.2-17 the first sync after an import sends them one by one, which takes minutes for a 200-card file. During that time a person can open the Contact Manager and fix a phone number on a card not sent yet. Their fix is overwritten when the sync reaches that card. If they delete a card instead, it comes back.

Group: this is a race with a narrow window, except after a bulk import, which happens once. The project's own audit graded the same race for tasks, notes and events as "should" (13.2-20's objective). Before 13.2-17 the same shape existed on the first full read, so 13.2 widened it rather than created it. "should" is the honest group.

Fix: the proposed transaction works but is more than needed, and it fixes only half the race. Smaller fix: one helper shared by both create blocks. After the create returns, read the row again with `cache.get_contact(&local.id)`.
- If it is gone, save the new identity and then call the existing `delete_contact`. That writes the Google or Outlook deletion note with code already in the repo.
- If its `updated_at` changed, save it with the new identity only and do not call `told`, so the change is still waiting.
- Otherwise, save as today.

The other half is not fixed by either version. The Contact Manager builds its save from the copy it read when it opened (`to_stored(.., replacing)`). If it opens before a create finishes and closes after, it erases the new Google identity and marks the contact waiting again. The next sync then creates the contact a second time at Google. Re-reading `replacing` when the manager saves would close that half.

findings.title: A kept contact whose card is gone fails on every sync
findings.what_this_is: After a whole read, take_off_who_a_whole_answer_left_out removes the contacts that the address book no longer holds. It keeps one that has a change waiting here.
findings.problem: The contact it keeps still carries the address book's name for someone who no longer exists there. Every sync pushes the change to that name and is refused every time: 404 from Google and Outlook, 412 (a failed version check) from CardDAV because of If-Match. Nothing ever ends this, although the doc comment says she stays "as a change kept here stays".
findings.concrete_case: Ann is deleted on the phone, and the same day she is edited here. On CardDAV, where every read is whole, or after Google's marker expires, Ann is kept. From then on every sync writes "The change to contact <id> could not be sent to ..." and counts one problem. The edit never reaches any server, and the id in the message does not tell the person which contact it is.
findings.fix: Keep her, but take that address book's name off and leave pending set: `cache.save_contact(&local.no_longer_in(address_book))`. The next push then creates her again with the edit, the way notes handle ItIsNotThere. The simpler choice is to drop her the way Google's own deletion report does, which already says that a change went with her.
findings.if_we_skip: That contact gives an error on every sync for good, and the person's edit never syncs.
findings.evidence: git show 0b781473:src/application/contacts_sync.rs L1325-1329: `if !left_out || the_copy_here_holds_work_nobody_has_sent(&local) || cache.is_held_for_a_choice(&local.id)? { continue; }`. L2358-2373: count_the_attempt turns any failed change into an error. Only deletions treat 404 as done (L2350-2352). carddav_sync.rs L299-304: a 412 is noted in still_built_on_an_old_copy and still counted as an error. The test helper only_the_dropped_person_went (added in 6ec6dd18) asserts that "local-waiting" stays, and nothing tests the sync after that.

findings.title: Contact names go into the log on every sync
findings.what_this_is: When Google or Outlook refuses to create a contact typed here, the sync records an error message.
findings.problem: The message contains the contact's name, and every contacts sync error is written to the log file. Since 13.2-17 the create runs on every sync, so a refused contact's name is logged again every few minutes. The rest of this module puts only the id in messages, on purpose.
findings.concrete_case: Google refuses to create "Dr Patel, oncology", for example because of a field it will not take. Every sync then writes `Failed to push contact 'Dr Patel, oncology' to Google: ...` to the log, which testers attach to bug reports.
findings.fix: Use `local.id` instead of `local.name` in both messages, as the CardDAV create already does (`Contact {} could not be added to {}`).
findings.if_we_skip: Personal names build up in log files that people share.
findings.evidence: git show 0b781473:src/application/contacts_sync.rs L2765-2767 `"Failed to push contact '{}' to Google: {}", local.name, e` and L2991-2993 for Microsoft. findings.title: A damaged compressed zip still gets the old 'stops partway through' sentence
findings.what_this_is: `WhyAnEntryWasNotRead` sorts a failed read by its error kind. Only InvalidData counts as "does not match what the archive records" (damaged or changed). Every other kind counts as "could not be read".
findings.problem: zip raises InvalidData only from its checksum and size checks. Most zips are compressed, including this program's own export, which writes Deflated. Damage inside compressed bytes is usually caught first by the decompressor, flate2, and it raises InvalidInput ("corrupt deflate stream"). So in the common real case, the new sentences from 13.2-31.7 and 13.2-31.8 are never reached. Every test damages a stored (uncompressed) entry, which hits only the checksum path.
findings.concrete_case: Case 1: a Deflated export whose Inbox.mbox has one bad byte at the 300 MB mark. The mail before that point comes in, then flate2 fails with InvalidInput. `a_stop_counted` reports "1 message in the archive could not be read, because there was nothing in it a mail program recognises", while thousands of messages are missing. Case 2: a small Deflated zip whose only entry is damaged in its first 64 KB is refused with "... stops partway through ... Ask the program that wrote it for another copy". Commit 23c0bbbc says it replaced exactly that sentence. Ledger 908 tracks the in-pieces wording for kinds other than InvalidData, but it treats them as a file that stopped being readable, not as damage, and it does not cover the look-over refusal.
findings.fix: Make it one line: `InvalidData | InvalidInput => Self::ItDoesNotMatchWhatTheArchiveRecords`. Add a case that writes 0xFF over the first compressed byte of a Deflated entry. That is an invalid block type, so it fails the same way every time.
findings.if_we_skip: People holding a damaged archive are told it was cut short and sent for another copy, or told one message failed when most of a folder is missing.
findings.evidence: flate2-1.1.9/src/zio.rs L155-157 and L235-237: `io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput, "corrupt deflate stream"`. zip-9.0.4/src/crc32.rs: InvalidData only at L45-48 (larger than declared) and L66 (Invalid checksum). Crc32Reader::read passes the decoder's error through with `?` (L71-72). mailbox_archive.rs L497-505 maps only InvalidData. The tests use `a_zip_of_stored_bytes` with `damaged_at_its_first` (L1837). importing_messages.rs L1106-1121 (`a_stop_counted`). The wording is pinned at import_tree.rs L1185. The 13.2-31.7 and 31.8 plans never mention InvalidInput or a Deflated entry (`git grep -i 'InvalidInput\|deflate stream'` over both plans finds nothing).

2. On any decoder error, flate2-1.1.9/src/zio.rs:153-158 returns `io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput, "corrupt deflate stream"`.

- Case 1 (the import path through `a_stop_counted`): ledger 908 is open for every stop of a kind other than `InvalidData`, and the changelog's Known limits (L1488-1490) states it. That part is ledgered.

So a Deflated entry whose packed data is broken counts as plain "could not be read".
